levels.title: Ask the Librarian
levels.story: Odile points at the whole catalogue and says: "Ask for exactly what you need, in words the shelves understand."

everyday.scene: At the library desk you say: "Mystery books, newest first, just the top three."
everyday.question: How would you say that to a computer?
everyday.answer: In SQL, the language for asking a database questions. That request becomes SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT.

lessons.title: SELECT and FROM
text: SQL is the language for asking a database questions. SELECT names the columns you want, and FROM names the table: SELECT title, year FROM books; gives two columns for every row. SELECT * means every column.
The answer to a query is itself a table. Asking does not change the stored data.

lessons.title: WHERE: choose the rows
text: WHERE keeps only the rows that pass a test: SELECT title FROM books WHERE year > 2010; keeps books after 2010. Join tests with AND and OR. Text goes in single quotes, like genre = 'Mystery'.
Rows that fail are left out of the answer. The table itself is untouched.

terms.meaning: A test that is true or false for each row.

predict.prompt: How many books does WHERE genre = 'Mystery' AND year > 2010 keep? Use the table on the first page.
predict.answer: Two: Quiet Harbour (2012) and The Last Ferry (2021).

lessons.title: ORDER BY and LIMIT
text: ORDER BY sorts the answer, smallest first unless you add DESC. LIMIT keeps only the first few rows after sorting.
SELECT title FROM books WHERE genre = 'Mystery' ORDER BY year DESC LIMIT 3; gives the three newest mysteries. Without ORDER BY, the DBMS promises no particular order.

text.text: PostgreSQL and SQLite use LIMIT. The SQL standard added FETCH FIRST in SQL:2008, which PostgreSQL also supports, and SQL Server uses TOP.

activities.prompt: Watch the DBMS test each book's year against year > 2010, and predict some rows.
activities.explain: WHERE tests every row on its own and keeps only the ones that pass, so the answer holds just the later books.

steps.say: The query is SELECT title FROM books WHERE year > 2010. The DBMS tests each row's year, one at a time, and keeps the rows that pass.
Row 1: the year is 1998. 1998 > 2010 is false, so the row is left out.
Row 2: the year is 2008. Does it pass the test year > 2010?

predict.prompt: Row 2 has the year 2008. Does it pass year > 2010?
hints: Compare the year with 2010.
Is 2008 bigger than 2010?

steps.say: Row 3: the year is 2015. 2015 > 2010 is true, so the row is kept.
Row 4: the year is 2012. Does it pass the test year > 2010?

predict.prompt: Row 4 has the year 2012. Does it pass year > 2010?
hints: Compare the year with 2010.
Is 2012 bigger than 2010?

steps.say: Row 5: the year is 2005. 2005 > 2010 is false, so the row is left out.
Row 6: the year is 2019. Does it pass the test year > 2010?

predict.prompt: Row 6 has the year 2019. Does it pass year > 2010?
hints: Compare the year with 2010.
Is 2019 bigger than 2010?

steps.say: Row 7: the year is 2021. 2021 > 2010 is true, so the row is kept.
Row 8: the year is 2001. Does it pass the test year > 2010?

predict.prompt: Row 8 has the year 2001. Does it pass year > 2010?
hints: Compare the year with 2010.
Is 2001 bigger than 2010?

steps.say: Done. 4 rows pass the test, so the answer has 4 rows.

activities.prompt: Put the parts of this query in the order SQL needs.
hints: SELECT starts the query, and LIMIT ends it.
WHERE comes right after FROM, and sorting comes after that.
activities.explain: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT: pick, source, filter, sort, cut.

activities.prompt: Which query lists the titles of books published after 2010?

options.text: SELECT title FROM books WHERE year > 2010;
SELECT year FROM books WHERE title > 2010;
WHERE year > 2010 SELECT title FROM books;

hints: The column you want goes after SELECT, and the test after WHERE.
The title is wanted, and the year is tested.
activities.explain: Wanted columns after SELECT, the table after FROM, and the test after WHERE.

activities.prompt: Using the table on the first page, how many rows does SELECT title FROM books WHERE genre = 'Reference' OR year > 2015; return?
hints: OR keeps a row if either test passes.
Reference books are 1 and 6. Books after 2015 are 6 and 7. Count the different books.
activities.explain: Books 1 and 6 are Reference, and books 6 and 7 are after 2015. Book 6 passes both, so 3 different rows.

activities.prompt: Match each clause to its job.
hints: Each word says what it does.
WHERE is about rows. SELECT is about columns.
activities.explain: Columns, table, rows, sort, cut.

activities.prompt: A query has no ORDER BY. Can you rely on rows coming back in the order they were added?

options.text: No, the order is not promised
Yes, always in the order added

hints: What does ORDER BY exist for?
If order were guaranteed, ORDER BY would be pointless.
activities.explain: Without ORDER BY the DBMS may return rows in any order. Ask for the order you need.

feed.explain: SELECT picks columns. FROM picks the table.

options.text: Only the rows that pass a test

feed.prompt: Why add ORDER BY before LIMIT 3?

options.text: Otherwise "first three" could be any three

feed.prompt: Write in words what ORDER BY year DESC LIMIT 1 gives.
feed.answer: The single newest row, by year.

fieldNotes.title: Every search box
fieldNotes.text: WHERE keeps only the rows that pass a test, and ORDER BY sorts what is left, so a query can filter and sort a list in one go.

fieldNotes.title: The answer is a table
fieldNotes.text: A query's result has rows and columns too, so it can feed into the next query or be shown on screen as a grid.

summary: You asked for columns with SELECT, filtered rows with WHERE, and sorted and trimmed the answer with ORDER BY and LIMIT.
Odile reads your first query and nods. "Specific. I like that."

mistake.title: Expecting an order you did not ask for
mistake.text: Rows can come back in any order if you do not say. When the order matters, always add ORDER BY.

levels.title: Count and Group
levels.story: Odile wants totals, not long lists: how many loans, and which readers borrow the most. Kit learns to squash rows into answers.

everyday.scene: At month's end the librarian wants one number per genre: how many loans each genre had, not the full list of loans.
everyday.question: How would a database produce that?
everyday.answer: By putting rows that share a genre into groups and counting each group. In SQL that is GROUP BY with COUNT.

lessons.title: Many rows, one answer
text: An aggregate function squashes many rows into one value. COUNT(*) counts rows, SUM adds a column, AVG averages it, and MIN and MAX find the smallest and largest.
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans; returns a single row holding 9 for our loans table. Aggregates other than COUNT(*) skip empty values.

terms.meaning: A function that turns many rows into one value.

predict.prompt: SELECT MAX(year) FROM books; returns how many rows?
predict.answer: One row, holding the biggest year, 2021.

lessons.title: GROUP BY: one answer per group
text: GROUP BY puts rows with the same value into a group, and the aggregate runs once per group. SELECT member_id, COUNT(*) FROM loans GROUP BY member_id; gives one row for each member who has borrowed.

text.text: In general, a column in SELECT must be named in GROUP BY or sit inside an aggregate.

references.title: PostgreSQL documentation: GROUP BY and HAVING

lessons.title: WHERE before, HAVING after
text: WHERE filters rows before they are grouped. HAVING filters whole groups after the counting is done. To find members with more than 2 loans you need HAVING COUNT(*) > 2, because the count only exists once groups are made.
WHERE chooses which rows go into the groups. HAVING chooses among the finished groups.

predict.prompt: Which clause can use COUNT(*) in its test: WHERE or HAVING?
predict.answer: HAVING. The counts only exist after grouping.

text.text: A query is processed roughly in this order: FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY and HAVING, then the select list. Sorting with ORDER BY comes last.

activities.prompt: The loans table has these loan counts per member: member 1 has 3, member 2 has 1, member 3 has 4, member 5 has 1. What does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans WHERE member_id = 3; return?
hints: Count only the loans made by member 3.
Look at member 3's count in the list.
activities.explain: Member 3 made 4 loans, so COUNT(*) returns 4.

activities.prompt: SELECT member_id, COUNT(*) FROM loans GROUP BY member_id; gives one row per member who has loans. Members 1, 2, 3 and 5 have loans. How many rows come back?
hints: One row per group.
Count the members who appear.
activities.explain: Four members have loans, so four groups and four rows.

activities.prompt: The loan counts are: member 1 has 3, member 2 has 1, member 3 has 4, member 5 has 1. How many rows does ... GROUP BY member_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 2; return?
hints: HAVING keeps the groups whose count passes the test.
Which counts are bigger than 2?
activities.explain: Members 1 (3) and 3 (4) pass, so 2 rows.

activities.prompt: Sort each test: does it belong in WHERE or in HAVING?
hints: Does the test use an aggregate like COUNT or AVG?
Aggregates only exist after grouping, so they go in HAVING.
activities.explain: Tests on single rows go in WHERE. Tests on counts, sums and averages of groups go in HAVING.

activities.prompt: Match each aggregate to what it returns.
hints: The names are short for their jobs.
SUM adds up, AVG averages.
activities.explain: Count, total, mean, smallest and largest.

activities.prompt: Put the steps in the order a query is worked out, in the usual teaching order.
hints: Rows are chosen before they are grouped.
Sorting the final answer comes last.
activities.explain: Pick the table, filter rows, group, filter groups, choose columns, then sort.

activities.prompt: The Mystery books have 310, 280 and 250 pages. What does SELECT AVG(pages) FROM books WHERE genre = 'Mystery'; return?
hints: Add the three page counts, then divide by how many there are.

activities.prompt: Why does WHERE COUNT(*) > 2 cause an error?

options.text: Counts are worked out after grouping, but WHERE runs before
COUNT cannot be used on loans

hints: Think about when the groups exist.
WHERE has finished before GROUP BY starts.
activities.explain: Use HAVING for tests on aggregates, since they only exist once groups are formed.

feed.prompt: To keep only groups with more than 2 rows, use...
What does GROUP BY member_id do?

options.text: Makes one group per member, so aggregates run once per group

feed.explain: Rows with the same member_id fall into one group.

feed.prompt: Explain the difference between WHERE and HAVING.
feed.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after counting.

fieldNotes.title: Totals per group
fieldNotes.text: GROUP BY combines rows that share a value into one group, so aggregates such as a count or a sum can be worked out for each group.

source.title: PostgreSQL docs: GROUP BY and HAVING

fieldNotes.title: Skipping empty values
fieldNotes.text: In SQLite, SUM and AVG ignore empty (NULL) values, while COUNT(*) counts every row in the group.

summary: You squashed many rows into one answer with aggregates, made one answer per group with GROUP BY, and filtered groups with HAVING.
Odile taps the sheet. "Now I can see what the readers really like."

mistake.title: Using WHERE for a count
mistake.text: A test like COUNT(*) > 2 belongs in HAVING, not WHERE, because the counts do not exist until the groups are made.

levels.title: Two Shelves at Once
levels.story: The loan slips hold only numbers. To read names and titles, Kit has to look at two shelves at once.

everyday.scene: A loan slip says "member 3, book 7". The desk wants a printout that reads "Chi borrowed The Last Ferry".
everyday.question: How could a database build that sentence from two tables?
everyday.answer: By joining: matching each loan's member_id to the same value in members, and its book_id to books. The matching columns are the keys you met earlier.

lessons.title: JOIN ... ON
text: A join combines rows from two tables where a condition holds. SELECT members.name, loans.borrowed FROM loans JOIN members ON loans.member_id = members.member_id; pairs each loan with the member it points at.
When both tables have a column of the same name, put the table name in front. The ON condition is nearly always a foreign key equal to a primary key.

terms.meaning: Combining rows of two tables where a condition holds.

lessons.title: Inner and left joins
text: An inner join keeps only rows that match on both sides, so members who never borrowed vanish from it. A left outer join keeps every row from the left table, and fills the right side with empty values, called NULL, where nothing matches.
Use LEFT JOIN for "all members, even those with no loans".

terms.meaning: Only rows that match on both sides.
Every left row, matched or not.

predict.prompt: Six members, of whom four have borrowed. How many different members show up in an inner join of members and loans?
predict.answer: Four. Dev and Fay have no loans, so they drop out.

lessons.title: Chaining joins, and a trap
text: To show who borrowed which title, chain two joins: loans to members, then loans to books. Each JOIN has its own ON.
If two tables are listed with no matching condition, every row pairs with every row. Our 6 members and 9 loans would give 54 nonsense rows. Always check the row count looks sensible.

terms.meaning: Every row of one table paired with every row of another.

activities.prompt: How many rows does SELECT * FROM loans JOIN members ON loans.member_id = members.member_id; return? (There are 9 loans, and each points at one real member.)
hints: Each loan matches exactly one member.
One output row per loan.
activities.explain: Every loan matches one member, so 9 rows.

activities.prompt: Members: 6. Loans: 9, made by 4 of those members. How many rows does SELECT * FROM members LEFT JOIN loans ON loans.member_id = members.member_id; return?
hints: Matched members appear once per loan.
Each of the two members with no loans appears once, with empty values.
activities.explain: 9 rows for the matched loans, plus 1 each for Dev and Fay, makes 11.

activities.prompt: A query lists 6 members and 9 loans with no matching condition. How many rows come back?
hints: Every member pairs with every loan.
Multiply 6 by 9.
activities.explain: 6 × 9 = 54 rows of mostly nonsense pairs.

activities.prompt: Sort each member: do they appear in an inner join of members and loans, or only in the left join?
hints: An inner join needs a match on both sides.
Which members have no matching loan?
activities.explain: Members with loans match in both joins. Dev and Fay show up only when the left side is kept whatever happens.

activities.prompt: Put the parts of this query in order.
hints: SELECT first, then FROM, then each JOIN.
Sorting goes last.
activities.explain: Choose the columns, name the starting table, add each join, then sort.

activities.prompt: Which ON condition matches each loan to the book it points at?
hints: Match a foreign key to the primary key it points at.
Which loans column holds a book's id?
activities.explain: book_id in loans is the foreign key, and book_id in books is the primary key.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.right: Only rows with a match on both sides
Every left row, matched or not
The condition that decides which rows pair up
An empty value where nothing matched

hints: A left join never drops a left row.
NULL appears where the right side has nothing.
activities.explain: Inner needs both sides, left keeps its left rows, ON sets the pairing, NULL marks the gaps.

activities.prompt: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans JOIN books ON loans.book_id = books.book_id WHERE books.title = 'The Lost Lantern'; The Lost Lantern is book 2, and loans 1, 3, 7 and 9 point at it. What number comes back?
hints: Join first, then keep only the loans of that title.
Count the loans that point at book 2.
activities.explain: Four loans point at book 2, so the count is 4.

options.text: A foreign key with the primary key it points at

feed.explain: That is how rows from two tables find each other.

feed.prompt: Which join keeps left rows with no match?
feed.explain: A left join keeps every left row and fills gaps with NULL.

feed.prompt: Why is a missing matching condition dangerous?

options.text: Every row pairs with every row, giving a huge nonsense result

feed.prompt: When would you pick LEFT JOIN over an inner join?
feed.answer: When you want every row from the left table, even those with no match, like all members including those with no loans.

fieldNotes.title: Joins bring tables together
fieldNotes.text: A joined table is built from two other tables by matching their rows with a join condition. That is how a table of ids can be combined with another table to bring in names and titles.

fieldNotes.title: Empty means unknown
fieldNotes.text: A left join fills gaps with NULL. NULL means "no value here", which is different from zero or an empty word.

summary: You joined tables with a key match, saw the difference between inner and left joins, and spotted why a missing condition explodes the row count.
Odile closes the last drawer. "Two shelves, one answer. Well done, Kit."

mistake.title: Forgetting the matching condition
mistake.text: Two tables with no matching condition pair every row with every row. When a result has far too many rows, check the ON first.
